list.listitem: Suspect hallux valgus (bunion) in a patient who presents with history of progressive forefoot pain and a bump or lateral deviation of the great toe seen on examination. C
Confirm this with weight-bearing radiographs. C
For mildly symptomatic patients, recommend anti-inflammatory medications and orthotics. C
Refer patients who are refractory to conservative measures for surgical evaluation; no particular surgery is preferred. B

background.definition: Hallux valgus is a deformity of the forefoot in which medial prominence of the first metatarsal head and lateral deviation of the great toe is noted. A bunionette, also called a tailor’s bunion, refers to a similar deformity of the lateral side of the fifth toe.

list.listitem: Among 2,446 adults aged 39 to 99 years (mean 66 years) from the Framingham Foot Study, the prevalence of hallux valgus was 31% and the prevalence of lesser toe deformities was 29.6%.
Females are affected more frequently than males.
Bunions are associated with increasing age, although they can occur in adolescents; occurrence peaks in the third to fifth decades.
Hallux valgus is associated with falls in the elderly (pooled odds ratio 1.89, 95% confidence interval 1.19-3.00).
Gait changes due to pain from hallux valgus can cause increased abductor moments at the knee increasing medial load and potentially predisposing to knee osteoarthritis.

Unknown; possible inherited component; in one case series, 83% had a family history. In the Framingham Foot Study, significant heritability was found ranging from 0.29 to 0.89, depending on age and sex (0 = no genetic contribution).
Improper footwear.
Underlying foot pathology (see Risk Factors below).
In the forefoot, medial tension causes the medial collateral ligaments to pull on the dorsomedial aspect of the first metatarsal head.
The sesamoid apparatus may dislocate laterally.
Remodeling occurs laterally and medially, resulting in an increase in the bony prominence of the foot at the first metatarsophalangeal joint.
Suspect hallux valgus in patients with deformity and in some cases pain of the first metatarsal. C
Obtain weight-bearing radiographs of the affected foot. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Multiple joints may be affected; ±effusion; osteophytes on radiographs may coexist
Often acute attack (within hours); joint red, hot, tender; tophi may be present
History of force applied to affected area

list.listitem: Patients with hallux valgus commonly complain of deformity and pain at the first metatarsophalangeal joint. They may also describe a burning pain or tingling at the site.
Obtain history from the patient including family history of similar problem and whether the forefoot deformity is progressive and painful.

Examine the affected foot, looking for presence/absence of a bunion, lateral deviation of the great toe, abnormal range of motion of the first metatarsophalangeal joint, painful joint, and widened forefoot.
Clinical examination of the foot typically reveals a bony prominence or medial bump at the first metatarsophalangeal joint. The great toe is abducted or deviated laterally.
The preoperative hallux valgus angle is a good predictor of the postoperative angle.
Obtain radiographs of the affected foot in a weight-bearing stance and with the patient standing in the angle and base of gait.
If diagnosis is uncertain, consider uric acid, sedimentation rate, or screening labs.
Suspect hallux valgus in patients with deformity and pain of the first metatarsal. Pain may not occur until the deformity has advanced. Pain alone does not characterize the condition.
Obtain radiographs to look for medial prominence of the first metatarsal head, presence of osteoarthritis, abnormal hallux abductus angle (>15°-20°), and abnormal intermetatarsal angle (>9°).
In the initial treatment, include wider, flatter shoes, bunion pads, orthoses, and NSAIDs.
Consider surgical options if supportive treatment does not lead to symptom improvement.
Anti-inflammatory medications along with orthotics may help relieve symptoms in mild to moderate cases. C
Refer patients unresponsive to conservative measures for surgical evaluation. B
NSAIDs may be used to improve discomfort during acute, painful episodes.

Corticosteroid injections (less commonly) may be used to decrease inflammation at the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Authors of a randomized trial of 60 patients, 50 of whom completed the study, found less oxycodone consumption in those randomized to 9 mg oral dexamethasone give preoperatively and 24 hours postoperatively (45 vs. 78 tablets). Patients also reported less pain and nausea, especially early.

Surgical therapy may be offered when conservative therapy fails to relieve patient symptoms. In an RCT of 209 patients with bunions, patients randomized to surgery had slightly less pain and disability than those randomized to orthotics or watchful waiting, but time lost from work increased as did cost of treatment. Quality of life scores did not differ between groups.

One trial demonstrated that surgery gave 10% improvement in function and a 50% improvement in pain compared with orthoses or no treatment. Authors of a systematic review of surgical treatment for hallux valgus found low postoperative patient dissatisfaction of 10% and 1.5% reported postoperative first metatarsophalangeal pain.
Surgery is contraindicated in patients with vascular insufficiency or active infection of the foot.
Routine submission of surgical specimens for histopathology is not recommended, with only 1 new diagnosis in a series of over 300 cases.

The specific procedure chosen depends on the surgeon's preference, degree of deformity, and specific patient characteristics. Surgical procedures range from capsular tendon balancing or exostectomy, osteotomy, resection arthroplasty with or without implant, first metatarsophalangeal arthrodesis (i.e., fusion), and first metatarsocuneiform joint arthrodesis. Authors of a systematic review found no evidence that one procedure was better than another, although the overall study quality is poor. Another systematic review identified 3 studies of percutaneous and minimum incision metatarsal osteotomy, but all were case series of limited quality.

A systematic review identified 6 RCTs and one non-randomized comparative study with a total of 395 feet comparing minimally invasive surgery (incision < 2 cm) with standard open surgery. They found no advantage to minimally invasive surgery.

Authors of a systematic review of 28 studies found high patient satisfaction rates following both proximal osteotomies and distal and diaphyseal osteotomies (100% and 92%, respectively). Another systematic review found no significant difference in outcomes between patients treated with Scarf or chevron osteotomies.
Similar outcomes were reported in two RCTs comparing proximal with distal chevron osteotomy, both with supplementary lateral soft-tissue release, for moderate to severe hallux valgus deformity.

One RCT found the Scarf osteotomy to be superior to Ludloff osteotomy in pain (at best) and radiologic measures, but functional outcomes and patient satisfaction were similar. In an RCT with 20 patients, Scarf osteotomy had similar outcomes to the minimally invasive SERI distal metatarsal osteotomy with respect to early anatomic correction and American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Scores.

Proximal chevron osteotomy and proximal opening wedge osteotomy of the first metatarsal also resulted in similar operative and clinical outcomes in a RCT of patients with hallux valgus with an increased intermetatarsal angle. Women with hallux valgus randomized to chevron osteotomy, however, had significantly better results on clinical score, number of postoperative complications, patient satisfaction, and length of sick leave at 3 years compared to those undergoing Mitchell's osteotomy.

A meta-analysis of ten studies showed increased intermetatarsal angle correction from proximal chevron osteotomy compared to the distal osteotomy. This same analysis found distal chevron osteotomies result in greater hallux metatarsal phalangeal angle correction compared to the scarf procedure.

In an RCT of 100 patients undergoing chevron osteotomy, function score was better in the group treated without osteotomy fixation and with an elastic bandage vs. short cast at 6 weeks postoperatively, but no differences were found in the longer term.

Data, primarily from case series, are also limited on minimally-invasive surgical techniques including arthroscopy, percutaneous, and minimum-incision surgery. In one case series of 72 patients undergoing minimally invasive distal metatarsal osteotomy, 16 (18.8%) deformity recurrences were noted with an overall complication rate of 29.4%. Poorer preoperative congruence of the metatarsophalangeal joint and tibial sesamoid position correlated with a higher rate of recurrence. In a small RCT of 47 patients with hallux valgus, minimally invasive chevron osteotomy was comparable to the open chevron technique with respect to radiological, American Orthopedic Foot and Ankle Society forefoot scores and patient satisfaction.

Clinical and radiological outcomes were similar in one RCT comparing the Lapidus procedure, which includes arthrodesis of the first tarsometatarsal joint, to a simple Hohmann distal closing wedge metatarsal osteotomy at a mean of 9.25 years follow-up.

In one systematic review of arthrodesis (almost half performed for severe hallux valgus), nonunion occurred in 5.4% (153 of 2,818), symptomatic in about 1/3rd of cases (50 of 153), and malunion in 6.1%. In a more recent meta-analysis of 29 studies of first tarsometatarsal joint arthrodesis for moderate to severe hallux valgus deformity, the overall complication rate was 16% with a nonunion rate of 4%.
Radiographic and clinical outcomes were similar for use of a biodegradable magnesium-based screw compared with titanium screws for mild hallux valgus deformities treated with osteosynthesis.

Adults with moderate to severe subluxated hallux valgus deformities may be candidates for proximal crescentic osteotomy of the first metatarsal combined with distal soft tissue realignment. Authors of a case series found significant pain improvement and minimal recurrence of deformity in subjects studied, with 93% of patients rating results as good or excellent.

In a small RCT of patients with painful hallux valgus, both Botulinum Toxin type A (BTXA) and control (saline) injections into the oblique and transverse heads of the adductor hallucis, flexor hallucis brevis and extensor hallucis longus muscles resulted in improved pain and disability at 1 month. However, only patients receiving BTXA injections had persistent improvement at 2 and 6 months after treatment.

One study with 66 patients found lower post-operative pain scores with use of peripheral nerve stimulation for patients undergoing ankle or foot surgeries. This could be beneficial for post-operative pain management.
Recommend a change to flatter, wider shoes, and weight loss if indicated.

Prescription orthotics may help control foot biomechanics in early stages of hallux valgus. However, authors of a systematic review found only 3 studies (total of 332 patients) of conservative treatments like orthoses, and no difference in outcomes between treated and untreated patients; this Cochrane review has been withdrawn.
An insole with toe separator may decrease pain intensity, but does little to improve the great toe angle.

For patients with mild to moderate hallux valgus, splints can be used; one small RCT showed a greater decrease in hallux valgus angles with researcher-designed slipper splints vs. nonprescription splints.
Manual and manipulative therapy was equivalent to standard care with night splints for short-term outcomes in one RCT of 60 patients with symptomatic mild to moderate hallux valgus.
Refer patient for surgical evaluation if conservative measures have not controlled symptoms.
Hallux valgus is a progressive condition that is likely precipitated by poor footwear and underlying foot pathology. It may improve with treatment, although long-term follow-up studies are lacking. C
Mild to moderate cases may benefit from conservative treatment. B

Patients who undergo surgical intervention report less pain. B Authors of a case series found that changes in radiographic angles were not correlated with patient-centered outcomes following hallux valgus surgery.

In several case series cited by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, recurrence rates following surgery were 1% and 2%. In another case series, 95% of patients were pain free at a mean follow-up of 9 years. However, in a case series of 118 patients (162 feet) who underwent surgery for hallux valgus, at a mean of 5.2 years, only 53 feet (32.7%, in 43 patients) were completely asymptomatic and 25.9% of patients dissatisfied with the outcome.
Based on one study, the risk of recurrence is greater and function worse if the preoperative hallux valgus angle exceeds 30°.
One study analyzing long-term recurrence rates of hallux valgus found that Mitchell osteotomies resulted in a significantly higher rate of recurrence compared to Chevron and Bosch osteotomies.

Progress can be followed using the Foot and Ankle Outcome Score which has been validated for use in patients with hallux valgus and shows moderate correlation with with two physical health related SF-12 domains.

In a case series of 20 children, chevron osteotomy was an effective procedure to correct juvenile hallux valgus deformity. At 7 year follow-up with 12 patients, there was good functional performance measured by the AOFAS, unlimited walking, and few patients reported pain with weather changes.

In a second case series of 18 children undergoing percutaneous surgery, 20 (61%) feet had hallux valgus angle values greater than 16° (under correction), but in half these cases, the patients reported being satisfied with the procedure.
If conservative management fails, surgery should be delayed until skeletal maturity is reached for optimal deformity correction.
